title: Trucking / motor-carrier niche commercial insurance agency (owner-operators and small fleets)
subindustry: Commercial P&C retail agency - trucking/commercial auto
product_service: Placement and servicing of auto liability, physical damage, motor truck cargo, GL, occupational accident/WC and federal/state filings for for-hire carriers with 1-25 power units; certificate issuance and filing maintenance.
target_customer: Owner-operators and small fleets (1-25 trucks) with own authority, Midwest/national; dispatchers and factoring companies as referral sources.
purchase_motivation: Federal/state minimum financial responsibility filings are a condition of operating authority; shippers/brokers demand COIs; premiums are a top-3 cost so carriers shop at renewal.
spending_evidence: ATRI: truck insurance premiums averaged 10.6 cents/mile in 2025 (~$10k/truck at an assumed ~100k miles/yr [E]), and small fleets pay nearly double per mile vs large fleets [C, WS02-S017].
representative_operators: Thousands of small trucking-focused retail agencies (unnamed in our sources) [E]
Large brokers with transportation practices, e.g. Brown & Brown (35.9% adj. EBITDAC margin, incumbent economics) [B, WS02-S009]
revenue_mechanism: % commission on premium paid by carrier/MGA (direct bill) plus possible agency/broker fees where lawful; renewal commissions annually.
typical_transaction_value: Premium roughly $10k-$25k per power unit per year (established fleets ~$10k at ATRI cents/mile; new ventures higher) [C/E]; commission ~10-16% direct or lower via wholesaler -> ~$1,000-$2,500 per truck per year [B/E, WS02-S016].
direct_costs: Producer/CSR labor (licensed CSRs), aggregator/wholesaler commission splits, lead data/telemarketing, E&O, agency management system, comparative rater.
contribution_profit_note: A 5-truck account at ~$15k/truck premium and ~10% commission yields ~$7.5k/yr commission before servicing labor; servicing filings/COIs/claims for trucking is labor-heavy [E].
working_capital_note: Commissions typically paid monthly after premium collection (direct bill); trucking cancellations for non-payment trigger return-commission chargebacks; agency-bill accounts create premium trust obligations [E].
sales_cycle: Days to weeks around authority activation or renewal; renewal shopping 30-60 days before expiry [E].
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: annual renewals, but new-venture trucking accounts churn heavily (authority revocations, business failures) [E].
acquisition_channels: FMCSA public licensing & insurance data on new/renewing authorities (outbound calling)
Referral partnerships with dispatch services, factoring companies, CDL schools, truck dealers
Spanish/Polish/Eastern-European language community marketing in Chicagoland
SEO for niche (hotshot, box truck, reefer) quotes
customer_accessibility: High identifiability (public USDOT/MC data) but heavily saturated by telemarketers; trust and speed decide [E].
supplier_accessibility: Assumed accessible but unconfirmed: a brand-new agency rarely gets direct appointments; realistic routes are aggregators/networks (SIAA claims start-up carrier access 'from day one' [D, WS02-S013]; Smart Choice markets no fees and a commission split until 'Leadership' level [D, WS02-S014]; fees/departure terms anecdotally material [D, WS02-S015]), branch/MGA platforms that recruit start-ups (TWFG passes ~60% of commission income to its agents [A, WS02-S012]) and E&S wholesalers. Illinois-specific aggregator terms MISSING. Trucking capacity for new ventures is concentrated in a few carriers/MGAs and tightens after nuclear verdicts [E].
competitive_intensity: high - many small agencies, captive programs, and national trucking specialists chase the same FMCSA leads [E].
entry_strategy: Pick a sub-niche (e.g., Chicago-area box-truck/last-mile carriers or a language community), offer same-day filings/COIs and safety/claims coaching that lowers premiums at renewal; bundle compliance help (UCR, IFTA reminders) as a retention tool.
licenses: Illinois resident producer license with Property and Casualty lines: 20 hrs pre-licensing per line (7.5 classroom), General+State Pearson VUE exams per line, $215 state fee per ~2-yr term, age 18+ [A, WS02-S001, WS02-S002, WS02-S003]; agency business-entity license $150 with a designated responsible licensed producer [A, WS02-S003]; carrier appointments (direct or via aggregator/wholesaler); E&O not found as an Illinois statutory mandate but expected by carriers/aggregators (TWFG branches pay their own E&O) [E; A, WS02-S012]; surplus line producer license (surety bond, SLAI membership, 3.5% tax + 0.04% stamping fee) only if placing E&S directly rather than through a licensed wholesaler [A/C, WS02-S004, WS02-S005].
regulatory_barriers: Producer licensing is modest; FMCSA tightened authority vetting in 2026 (Motus registration; automated screening of new/reinstated authority applications), which may shrink new-venture volume [C, WS02-S030].
operational_risks: Claims-heavy servicing; carrier/MGA withdrawal from trucking; E&O exposure on filings; high account churn.
financial_risks: Return commissions on cancellations; book value impaired by churn; carrier concentration.
geographic_constraints: Can write nationally with non-resident licenses ($380 Illinois non-resident fee indicates typical cost scale; each state differs) [A, WS02-S003]; Chicago is a large trucking hub [E].
founder_expertise: Commercial auto underwriting basics, FMCSA filings (BMC-91X, MCS-90), carrier appetites, claims handling; producer licensing.
staffing: Founder sells; first licensed CSR at ~150-250 accounts; second producer in year 2-3 [E].
automation_potential: AI can pre-fill applications from FMCSA/telematics data, generate COIs, chase loss runs, triage renewals; underwriting negotiation and claims advocacy stay human.
delegation_potential: Moderate-good: licensed CSRs and producers are a standard labor pool; account relationships can be institutionalized.
scalability: Book compounds via renewals; multi-state expansion via non-resident licenses; ceiling limited by carrier capacity and churn.
expansion: Cargo/occupational accident programs, fleet safety consulting, premium finance partnership, eventual MGA/program for a trucking sub-niche (WS02-016).
roic_note: Capital at risk mostly founder time plus $8k-$40k; if year-3 profit reaches $100k+, ROIC >200%; a renewal book is a sellable asset (sub-$1M-EBITDA agencies trade far below the 11.4x seen in >$1M-EBITDA deals) [C, WS02-S007].
critical_assumptions: A new agency can obtain trucking markets via aggregator/MGA/wholesaler within 3-6 months
Commission on trucking via intermediaries remains ~8-15%
Retention after year 1 can exceed ~70% in chosen sub-niche
unanswered_questions: Which aggregators/MGAs accept Illinois start-up agencies for trucking and on what split?
Actual new-venture trucking commission rates via wholesalers
FMCSA monthly new-authority counts after 2026 vetting changes
Small trucking book valuation multiples (revenue multiple)
failure_modes: Churn of new-venture truckers erodes book faster than sales add
Carrier exits leave agency without markets
E&O claim on a missed filing

title: Light-industrial / warehouse temporary staffing (Chicago-area, DTLSA-regulated)
subindustry: Temporary help — light industrial, warehouse, food production
product_service: W-2 temporary workers (pickers/packers, machine operators, assemblers, forklift operators, sanitation) supplied to client sites at an hourly bill rate; agency is employer of record and handles recruiting, payroll, taxes, workers' comp and DTLSA compliance.
target_customer: Plant, warehouse and HR managers at 50–1,000-employee manufacturers, 3PLs and food processors in Cook, DuPage, Will, Kane and Lake counties.
purchase_motivation: Variable/peak demand, absenteeism coverage, outsourcing high-turnover hourly recruiting, try-before-hire.
spending_evidence: US staffing firms employed ~2.0M temp/contract workers per week in Q4 2025 [C, WS12-S013]; SIA forecasts US industrial staffing revenue +7% in 2026 [C, WS12-S014]; the DTLSA amendments target >650,000 temporary workers in Illinois [A, WS12-S001]; PeopleReady (TrueBlue) alone billed $883.9M in 2025 [B, WS12-S010].
representative_operators: TrueBlue/PeopleReady — 2025 segment revenue $883.9M, segment profit $6.5M (~0.7%) [B, WS12-S010]
Hundreds of independent Chicago-area agencies on IDOL's 2026 registered-agency list [A, WS12-S004]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate = pay rate × markup covering FICA, FUTA/SUTA, workers' comp, DTLSA compliance cost and margin; billed weekly for hours worked; occasional conversion fees.
typical_transaction_value: Per worker roughly $21–26/hr billed on ~$16–18/hr pay → ~$40–50k annual billing per full-time temp [E]; a typical small client uses 5–40 temps.
direct_costs: Wages; employer FICA 7.65%; FUTA/IL SUTA; workers' comp (industrial classes — Illinois rates MISSING); compensable DTLSA safety training; equal-pay uplift after 720 hrs; benefits cash-equivalent after 720 hrs; transportation if provided.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbent gross margin 22.8% and SG&A 23.0% of revenue at TrueBlue → ~0.7% adjusted EBITDA [B, WS12-S010]. New entrant est. ~$3–5 gross profit per worker-hour → ~$6–10k GP per full-time temp-year; ~80–120 temps on billing needed to cover a minimal branch [E].
working_capital_note: Weekly payroll vs. client net-30 to net-60 → 5–9 weeks of payroll float; factoring advances 75–95% at ~1–5% of invoice [D, WS12-S016, WS12-S017]; WC carriers may demand deposits; payroll-tax trust-fund liability is personal risk.
sales_cycle: 2–8 weeks for owner-managed plants; larger sites buy via MSP/VMS with vendor qualification.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — weekly billing on open orders, but very high worker churn (2025 industry turnover 376%) [C, WS12-S013]
acquisition_channels: Job boards and community recruiting for worker supply
customer_accessibility: Buyers are identifiable and reachable, but most already run 2–5 agencies; displacing an incumbent requires better fill rates on hard shifts.
supplier_accessibility: Labor supply is the real supply chain: continuous recruiting needed; confirmed available but costly to retain [E].
competitive_intensity: extreme — national incumbents earn <1% EBITDA and hundreds of local agencies compete on price.
entry_strategy: Niche fill (2nd/3rd shift, food-grade sanitation, bilingual crews) with on-site coordinator and DTLSA-clean compliance as a selling point to risk-averse clients now jointly exposed under the Act.
licenses: IDOL DTLSA registration before operating: annual fee $3,000 per agency + $750 per branch, surety bond, client re-verification Mar 1/Sep 1 [A, WS12-S004]; equal pay after >720 hours at the same client in 12 months (PA 103-1030; clock from Apr 1, 2024) [C, WS12-S003]; equal benefits or hourly cash equivalent after >720 hours — preliminary injunction DENIED May 22, 2025, so enforceable [A, WS12-S001]; annual per-client general safety training at agency cost, compensable time [A, WS12-S006]; Section 67 'interested party' suits held unconstitutional by Cook County circuit court (Mar & May 2026), on appeal; IDOL not issuing right-to-sue notices meanwhile [A, WS12-S004; C, WS12-S005]. Plus IL Dept. of Employment Security UI account, workers' comp policy (IL rates for industrial classes MISSING).
regulatory_barriers: Illinois is the most demanding state for this segment: equal pay/benefits calculations depend on client data; joint client liability; record-keeping and notice duties; litigation history 2023–2026 [A, WS12-S001; A, WS12-S004].
operational_risks: Workplace injuries and WC claims; no-shows; DTLSA notice/training errors; client concentration; on-site safety failures attributed to agency.
financial_risks: Thin margin plus WC loss development can wipe out a year's profit; bad debt; payroll tax liabilities; dependence on factoring.
geographic_constraints: Branch radius ~20–30 miles; Illinois law applies to Illinois placements.
founder_expertise: Payroll tax, workers' comp risk management, DTLSA compliance, labor recruiting (Spanish strongly helpful).
staffing: Recruiter/dispatcher from day 1; on-site coordinator per large client; payroll/compliance admin by ~50 temps.
automation_potential: Shift-confirmation apps, AI applicant screening, scheduling and timekeeping reduce coordinator time; recruiting, retention, safety and client relationships remain human. AI substitution risk to demand: low near term (robotics slow), but software lowers barriers for app-based competitors.
delegation_potential: Branch-manager model is standard in the industry; delegable after ~2 years.
scalability: Branch replication possible but each branch needs WC collateral and payroll float; returns thin.
expansion: On-site managed programs, payrolling, skilled trades (WS12-002).
roic_note: Capital tied up in payroll float and WC collateral (~$60–150k at $2–3M revenue) [E]; at 2–5% operating margin ROIC is modest and volatile.
critical_assumptions: New entrant can price at 30–40% markup despite incumbents
WC premiums for warehouse/factory classes in IL are affordable for a new policy
Clients supply comparator wage/benefit data needed for 720-hour compliance
unanswered_questions: Illinois workers' comp loss costs/rates for classes 8292, 3632, 2003 etc. for a new staffing account
Has the Seventh Circuit or Illinois Supreme Court ruled further on DTLSA §42/§67 since May 2026?
How have Chicago-area clients changed temp usage (assignment caps at 720 hrs) since April 2024?
Initial (vs renewal) DTLSA registration fee and bond amount
failure_modes: Large WC claim or experience-mod spike
Client non-payment while payroll keeps running
DTLSA wage/benefit miscalculation leading to back-pay claims
Losing anchor client to a cheaper agency

title: Tariff-driven reshoring/nearshoring sourcing agent for importers (US & Mexico supplier transition)
product_service: Supplier search, RFQs, landed-cost and tariff comparison, supplier qualification (FAI/PPAP), and transition management for importers moving castings, forgings, machined, molded or fabricated components from Asia to US or USMCA-qualifying Mexican suppliers. Paid as a project fee plus success fee, or as ongoing broker margin.
target_customer: Purchasing/supply-chain managers at small-to-mid US importers and OEMs ($10-300M revenue) buying imported components.
purchase_motivation: Section 301 duties of generally 10-12.5% on 60 partners effective Jul 24, 2026 [C, WS03-S010]; 50% Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper [C, WS03-S011]; USMCA-qualifying goods excluded [C, WS03-S010]; policy volatility after IEEPA tariffs were struck down [C, WS03-S009, WS03-S033].
spending_evidence: Indirect only: trade press reports Protolabs network margins hurt by tariff inefficiencies [C, WS03-S003]. Fees actually paid for reshoring sourcing services are MISSING.
representative_operators: Xometry/Fictiv offer domestic and offshore networks [B, WS03-S001; C, WS03-S004]
Independent reshoring consultants and sourcing agents - names and economics MISSING [E]
revenue_mechanism: Project fee $5-25k plus a success fee of 3-5% of first-year spend, or conversion to broker markup [E].
typical_transaction_value: $5,000-$25,000 project; success fees on $100k-$2M annual spend [E]
direct_costs: Founder/analyst time, travel to supplier sites (incl. Mexico), sample and inspection costs, tariff-classification advisory (licensed customs broker if needed).
contribution_profit_note: One $15k project at ~70% gross margin = ~$10k contribution [E].
working_capital_note: Retainers can be billed upfront. Success fees lag 3-12 months behind supplier transition.
sales_cycle: 2-6 months; decisions stall when tariff rulings are pending (Section 301 litigation at CIT [C, WS03-S010]).
repeat_purchase: occasional - project-based; can convert to recurring broker margin
acquisition_channels: Outreach to importers identifiable through public import records
Referrals from customs brokers and freight forwarders
customer_accessibility: Importers are identifiable, but credibility walls are high and the deciders are busy. Many will run the exercise in-house or with existing suppliers.
supplier_accessibility: US job shops reachable (see WS03-001). Mexican suppliers require travel and network building. Unconfirmed.
competitive_intensity: moderate - consultancies, freight forwarders, platforms, and OEMs' own purchasing
entry_strategy: Narrow on one commodity (e.g., machined aluminum or castings) and buyers in one region. Publish transparent landed-cost comparisons, then take execution risk by acting as broker.
licenses: None for sourcing advice. Customs brokerage (filing entries for others) requires a CBP customs broker license, so it must be referred out [E].
regulatory_barriers: Must avoid acting as an unlicensed customs broker; country-of-origin/USMCA rules-of-origin accuracy.
operational_risks: Tariff reversals erase the savings case mid-project; supplier transitions fail at first article.
financial_risks: Success fees uncollectable if customer reverses; demand collapses if tariffs fall.
geographic_constraints: National market; Mexico travel needed for nearshoring.
founder_expertise: Tariff/HTS basics, rules of origin, manufacturing process costing, supplier qualification.
staffing: Solo initially; later analysts. Execution staff overlap with WS03-001.
automation_potential: AI helps with landed-cost models, HTS research drafts, supplier discovery and RFQ packaging. Judgement, travel and negotiation stay human.
scalability: Limited as a standalone advisory business; scale comes from converting clients into WS03-001 broker revenue.
expansion: Feeds WS03-001/003. Possible Mexico supplier network as a moat.
roic_note: Capital trivial; returns depend on founder hours rather than capital [E].
critical_assumptions: Tariff differentials persist long enough to justify supplier switches
Importers pay outsiders rather than doing it in-house
unanswered_questions: What fees/success fees buyers actually pay
Durability of Section 301 duties after CIT litigation
Mexico supplier accessibility for a newcomer
failure_modes: Policy whiplash makes the savings case vanish
Clients take the supplier list and execute themselves

title: LTL/truckload freight bill audit, overcharge and cargo-claim recovery for mid-market shippers
product_service: Pre- or post-payment audit of LTL/TL freight invoices (rate vs. tariff/contract, freight class/density reclassification, reweigh, accessorials, duplicates), filing overcharge claims and cargo loss/damage claims with carriers; optional freight-payment processing.
target_customer: Controllers/logistics managers at manufacturers and distributors with ~$1-20M/yr LTL/TL spend and no TMS-based audit.
purchase_motivation: Billing errors are routine in LTL (reweigh/reclass); finance teams lack time to audit; recovered cash is found money.
spending_evidence: Freight audit & pay firms charge 15-25% of recovered savings or a flat per-invoice fee; unaudited programs lose 3-5% of freight spend to billing errors; LTL reweigh/reclass variances 5-25% per shipment [D, WS14-S021]. Incumbent claims 20% invoice error rate and up to 8% recovered savings [D, WS14-S022].
representative_operators: AFS Logistics - freight audit/payment incumbent [D, WS14-S022]
Nuvocargo - carrier publishing audit-fee benchmarks (not an auditor) [D, WS14-S021]
revenue_mechanism: 15-25% contingency on recoveries [D, WS14-S021] or per-invoice audit fee; optional payment-processing float/fee.
typical_transaction_value: Illustrative: $5M freight spend x 3-5% errors [D] = $150-250k recoverable x 20% = $30-50k/yr per client [E, derived].
direct_costs: Audit analysts, rating-engine/tariff data subscriptions, claim-filing labor.
working_capital_note: Contingency fees paid after carriers credit/refund (30-120 days); payment-processing variant requires funding float and bonding - avoid early.
sales_cycle: 1-3 months; free retrospective audit of a sample of past invoices as door-opener.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: ongoing monthly audit once embedded in AP workflow.
acquisition_channels: Outbound to controllers at manufacturers/distributors (industrial directories)
Partnerships with freight brokers/TMS vendors who don't audit
customer_accessibility: Identifiable buyers; moderate cycle; need access to freight invoices and carrier contracts/tariffs.
supplier_accessibility: Tariff/rating data (e.g., carrier base rates) assumed licensable; access terms unknown.
competitive_intensity: high - established audit & pay firms, TMS vendors with built-in audit, brokers bundling audit.
entry_strategy: Target shippers below $3M spend that incumbents deprioritize; combine LTL audit with parcel (WS14-001) into one 'transportation cost recovery' offer.
licenses: None for audit; freight payment services may face money-transmitter questions if handling client funds [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low; carrier claim time limits (overcharge/cargo claim filing windows) govern recoverability [E].
operational_risks: Classification rule changes and carrier dispute processes are labor-intensive; poor data quality from clients.
financial_risks: Recoveries shrink as client fixes root causes; fee disputes on 'found' errors.
founder_expertise: LTL pricing (classification/density, tariffs, accessorials), claims law basics (Carmack liability), audit tooling.
automation_potential: High: OCR/AI invoice extraction, BOL vs invoice matching, re-rating against contracts; human handles carrier disputes.
scalability: National; scale tied to analyst capacity and sales.
expansion: Parcel (WS14-001), freight procurement bids, claims-only service, payment processing later.
roic_note: Low capital; returns driven by client count; ROIC high if sales succeed.
critical_assumptions: Mid-market shippers without TMS audit still lose 3-5% to errors
15-25% contingency fee holds for small clients
Rating data can be obtained affordably
unanswered_questions: Share of mid-market shippers already using audit services
Effect of recent freight-classification changes on error rates
failure_modes: Recoveries too small per client to cover analyst labor

title: Exclusive marketplace distributor for small and mid-size U.S.-made brands
product_service: Signs exclusive (or primary) online-marketplace distribution agreements with $1M-$20M brands; buys their inventory at wholesale, owns listings, advertising, MAP enforcement and unauthorized-seller removal on Amazon, Walmart, Target Plus, etc.
target_customer: Owners/sales VPs of small and mid-size consumer brands (preferably U.S.-made consumables: food, pet, HPC, cleaning) that lack marketplace expertise or suffer from unauthorized resellers.
purchase_motivation: Brands want marketplace revenue, price integrity (MAP) and brand protection without hiring an in-house team or paying agency retainers.
spending_evidence: Pattern Group, which buys inventory from brand partners and resells on 60+ marketplaces, grew revenue from $1.37B (2023) to $2.50B (2025), $3.26B TTM [C, WS06-S010, WS06-S011]; 116% net revenue retention 2024 [C, WS06-S011].
representative_operators: Pattern Group (Nasdaq: PTRN) - $3.26B TTM revenue, ~44% gross margin, 1-5% operating margin [C, WS06-S010]
Smaller exclusive-reseller agencies exist (names/financials not verified this session) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Buy at wholesale (often 40-55% off MSRP, assumed) and resell; margin after marketplace fees and ad spend; sometimes supplemented by service fees.
direct_costs: Wholesale COGS, inbound freight, marketplace referral fees (8-17%) [B, WS06-S002], FBA/fulfillment fees [B, WS06-S001], advertising (8-15% of sales, assumed).
contribution_profit_note: Gross margin here = after COGS and marketplace fees, before ads. Pattern's incumbent gross margin ~44% with only 1-5% operating margin at scale [C, WS06-S010]; a lean new entrant might net 6-12% of revenue [E].
working_capital_note: Inventory purchased upfront (net-30 possible after track record); 45-90 days on hand; working capital grows ~15-25% of incremental revenue [E]; inventory financing likely needed beyond ~$1M revenue.
sales_cycle: 1-4 months per brand partnership; contracts often 1-3 years with performance clauses [E].
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract with brand (repeat POs); consumer replenishment if consumable brands
acquisition_channels: Outbound to brands found via trade shows (Expo West, Sweets & Snacks), Faire, regional grocery shelves
customer_accessibility: Brand owners are identifiable and reachable; the pitch is quantifiable (unauthorized sellers, lost Buy Box, poor content).
supplier_accessibility: Supplier = the brand partner; accessible if the founder can prove execution. Unknown how many brands accept exclusivity with an unproven firm.
competitive_intensity: high - agencies, Pattern, other exclusive resellers, and brands' own in-house teams
entry_strategy: Niche focus (e.g., Midwest U.S.-made food/pet/cleaning brands, insulated from import tariffs) plus data-driven audits showing lost revenue; start with 2-3 brands, prove lift, then add.
licenses: Illinois registration [A, WS06-S034]; FDA food facility registration if the firm itself holds food in its own warehouse (FBA-only holding may differ - verify) [A, WS06-S019].
regulatory_barriers: Low; product compliance remains the brand's responsibility contractually.
operational_risks: Brand churn when contract ends; Amazon account health; concentration in a few brands; brand goes in-house after you build the channel.
financial_risks: Inventory obsolescence, ad cost inflation, chargebacks; thin operating margin (Pattern 1.0% in 2025 [C, WS06-S010]).
geographic_constraints: National; Illinois location helps for Midwest brands and warehousing.
founder_expertise: Marketplace advertising/analytics (fits tech background), contract negotiation, inventory planning.
staffing: Marketplace/ads specialist and inventory analyst by ~$2M revenue; 3PL rather than own warehouse.
automation_potential: Pricing and MAP monitoring, unauthorized-seller detection, listing optimization, demand forecasting, prospect audits - all automatable with ordinary tools; brand relationships human.
delegation_potential: Good once SOPs exist; account management roles are a standard e-commerce labor market.
scalability: Repeatable per brand; Pattern shows the model scales to billions but with thin margins.
expansion: International marketplaces, retail media, brand acquisition later (holding-company fit).
roic_note: If net 8% on $3M revenue ($240k) with ~$500k working capital (much financed), equity ROIC could be 50-100% [E]; heavily dependent on inventory turns.
critical_assumptions: Small brands will grant exclusivity to a new firm
Net margin 6-12% achievable without Pattern-scale software
Brand retention over 2+ years
unanswered_questions: Typical exclusive-reseller contract terms and discount off MSRP for sub-$20M brands
Failure/churn rates of small exclusive-reseller agencies
Pattern's segment detail on new vs. existing partner profitability
failure_modes: Thin margins swallowed by ad inflation

title: Mobile fleet washing route (tractors, trailers, box trucks, vans, equipment) with wastewater capture
product_service: Scheduled on-site (often overnight) washing of tractors, trailers, straight trucks, delivery vans, buses and construction equipment, with reclaim mats/vacuum recovery; add-ons: aluminum brightening, undercarriage salt removal, degreasing, graffiti removal, decal-safe washing.
target_customer: Fleet/terminal managers at for-hire carriers (4,442 with 6-100 PU in the Chicago 8-county area [A, WS17-S001]), private fleets with branded trucks (food/beverage distribution, uniform, utilities), last-mile van operators, equipment owners, municipalities (bids).
purchase_motivation: Brand image for private fleets, road-salt corrosion control in Chicago winters, lighting/reflector visibility, customer requirements; avoids drivers' time at truck washes.
spending_evidence: No verified spend data gathered (MISSING). Fleet trailer base is large: 52,879 owned + 42,998 term-leased trailers among Chicago mid-size carriers [A, WS17-S001].
representative_operators: Fleet Clean USA - franchised mobile fleet washing (size/Item 19 not retrieved) [E]
Fleetwash - national fleet washing provider (not verified) [E]
Local independent operators (count unknown) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-unit wash price x frequency (weekly/biweekly/monthly) under standing schedules.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis: $25-$60 per tractor, $30-$75 per trailer, $15-$35 per van; a 40-unit customer washed biweekly ~$2,000-$4,000/mo [E - unverified]
direct_costs: Two-person crew labor (night work), water, detergents, fuel, equipment wear, wastewater recovery/disposal.
contribution_profit_note: A crew washing ~40-80 units/night at assumed prices could gross ~$1,500-$3,500/night; contribution after crew and supplies ~40-55% [E].
working_capital_note: Net-30 invoicing typical (assumed); minimal inventory.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks; trial wash then standing schedule.
acquisition_channels: Drive-by prospecting of truck yards (Elk Grove Village, Bensenville, Bolingbrook, Joliet)
customer_accessibility: Good - yards are visible and dense; decision maker is often the terminal or fleet manager.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed in principle: pressure washers, reclaim systems and chemicals are widely sold (vendors not evaluated).
competitive_intensity: moderate-high - low skill barrier; incumbents include franchisees, independents, in-house wash bays and truck-stop washes.
entry_strategy: Be the documented-compliant operator (wastewater capture, insurance, background-checked crews) for brand-conscious private fleets and municipalities that must avoid illicit-discharge liability.
licenses: Business registration, insurance; wastewater: MS4 ordinances must prohibit non-stormwater discharge and commercial washing is not an allowable flow [A, WS17-S013]; MWRD/municipal sewer discharge approvals MISSING.
regulatory_barriers: Wash-water capture and disposal; possible local permits; chemical handling.
operational_risks: Chicago winter freezing limits outdoor washing for weeks; night labor turnover; damage claims.
financial_risks: Washing is among the first discretionary cuts in freight recessions.
founder_expertise: Equipment, chemistry, wastewater compliance, crew management.
staffing: Crews of 2 from day one if founder is not washing; crew lead per truck.
automation_potential: Route optimisation, scheduling, photo proof-of-service, invoicing; washing itself is manual.
delegation_potential: Moderate - standard labor roles, but turnover high.
scalability: Add rigs per ~15-30 customers; regional ceiling.
expansion: Pressure-washing of facilities, equipment detailing, decal removal for fleet remarketing (WS17-011).
roic_note: Rigs $15-60k each; payback plausibly <1 yr if routes fill [E].
critical_assumptions: Fleets pay assumed per-unit prices
Winter downtime manageable
Wastewater can be disposed lawfully at reasonable cost
unanswered_questions: MWRD and municipal rules for disposing mobile wash water

title: Flatbed / open-deck brokerage for steel, building-materials and machinery shippers
